# Your first graph

Build a small synthesizer signal path. Mount it on a canvas, switch its layout, and focus a module by double-clicking it.

[Open this chapter in Loom](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/docs/)

[Try the interactive signal path](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/docs/)

## Install Loom

Start in an empty directory with Node.js 22.12 or newer and npm. Vite serves the example and resolves the SDK imports.

```bash
npm init -y
npm install https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/packages/09f1acc80980067406c49b806f00ea381c5acd8e/loom-core-0.1.0.tgz
npm install --save-dev vite
```

The install command matches this Studio build. Published releases use an exact npm version. Preview builds use their GitHub Pages archive. Commit the resulting lockfile with your app.

## Mount the graph

Save these three files in the same directory, or copy them from `node_modules/loom-core/docs/examples/` after installing the package. Give the canvas a CSS width and height so the renderer can measure it on the first draw.

`index.html`

```html
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Signal path</title>
</head>
<body>
  <canvas id="patch" aria-label="Signal path" style="display:block;width:100%;height:360px"></canvas>
  <script type="module" src="./main.ts"></script>
</body>
</html>
```

Each node has a unique string ID. Each connection names its source and target by ID. In this patch, two sound sources feed a mixer, which sends its output through a filter to an amplifier. The preview above runs this function.

`signal-path.ts`

```ts
import { createGraph, parchment, type GraphData } from 'loom-core'

export const signalPath: GraphData = {
  nodes: [
    { id: 'osc', label: 'Oscillator', kind: 'source' },
    { id: 'noise', label: 'Noise', kind: 'source' },
    { id: 'mixer', label: 'Mixer', kind: 'mix' },
    { id: 'filter', label: 'Filter', kind: 'tone' },
    { id: 'amp', label: 'Amplifier', kind: 'output' },
  ],
  links: [
    { source: 'osc', target: 'mixer' },
    { source: 'noise', target: 'mixer' },
    { source: 'mixer', target: 'filter' },
    { source: 'filter', target: 'amp' },
  ],
}

export function mountSignalPath(canvas: HTMLCanvasElement) {
  const graph = createGraph(canvas, {
    ...signalPath,
    theme: {
      ...parchment,
      labels: { alternateSide: true },
      kind: { source: '#976343', mix: '#436653', tone: '#5d7190', output: '#a94c32' },
      wires: { routing: 'straight', width: 1.5, opacity: 0.65 },
    },
    mode: 'lanes',
    layout: { blend: 1, laneOrder: ['source', 'mix', 'tone', 'output'], laneGap: 70, rowGap: 56 },
  })
  graph.on('open', id => graph.focus(id))
  return graph
}
```

The graph handle owns its GPU buffers, listeners and layout. In a component, call `destroy()` when the canvas unmounts. This standalone entry keeps the graph available if the browser restores the page from its back-forward cache.

`main.ts`

```ts
import { mountSignalPath } from './signal-path.js'

const canvas = document.querySelector<HTMLCanvasElement>('#patch')
if (!canvas) throw new Error('Add a canvas with id="patch" to the page.')
const graph = mountSignalPath(canvas)

window.addEventListener('pagehide', event => {
  if (!event.persisted) graph.destroy()
})
```

## Run it

```bash
npx vite
```

Open the local address printed by Vite. Drag a module or double-click one to focus it. A browser with WebGL2 can run the preview. A host can catch `WebGL2UnavailableError` and offer a list or card view when WebGL2 is unavailable.

## Choose your next guide

- To draw arrows, style a node by kind or change layouts, read [Layouts and styling](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/docs/drawing/index.md).
- To load Wikipedia topics on demand and follow Music into Orbit, read [Stream a Wikipedia atlas](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/docs/atlas/index.md).
- To drive edits from TypeScript or JSON, read [Edit a graph document](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/docs/editing/index.md).
- To give an assistant bounded reads and revision-checked writes, read [Build an AI graph tool](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/docs/ai-tooling/index.md).
- To profile the patch on your device or tune a much larger map, read [Measure graph performance](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/docs/performance/index.md) and [Optimise large graphs](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/docs/optimisations/index.md).

# Layouts and styling

Give nodes a visual vocabulary, arrange them in lanes or rings, and draw the direction of a connection.

[Open this chapter in Loom](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/docs/drawing/)

## Choose a layout

Use `graph.setMode('lanes')` for categories with a shared axis, `'orbit'` for distance from a selected node, `'cloud'` for a rotatable volume, or `'drift'` for force-directed placement. In Orbit, Loom uses the highest-degree node as the center until you select one.

`graph.setLayout({ blend: 1 })` puts movable nodes on their layout targets. At zero, forces control their positions. Intermediate values let the graph respond to dragging while it approaches its anchors. A node supplied with both `x` and `y` starts pinned unless you set `pinned: false`.

## Draw a connection

Use the optional wire renderer when you need arrows, traveling pulses, separate paths for parallel links, or self-loops. Pass the same `nodes` and `links` you would pass to the core renderer. Give parallel edges stable IDs so their visual order survives a data reorder.

`drawing.ts`

```ts
import type { GraphData } from 'loom-core'
import { createWireGraph, sketchbook } from 'loom-core/wires'

export function drawConnections(canvas: HTMLCanvasElement, data: GraphData) {
  const graph = createWireGraph(canvas, {
    ...data,
    theme: sketchbook,
    drawingStyle: { fill: 'hachure', roughness: 0.7, hatchSpacing: 5 },
    wireEffects: { direction: 'arrow', separation: 16 },
  })

  graph.on('select', id => {
    graph.setWireEffects({ direction: id ? 'flow' : 'arrow', scope: 'selected' })
  })
  return graph
}
```

The flow speed is measured in CSS pixels per second. The separation between parallel paths is also in CSS pixels. A selected-node effect applies to its incident links. Reduced motion displays a static arrow. Open the working controls to compare the treatments. [Try connection drawing in the studio →](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/studio/?example=wires#settings-style)

## Map data to appearance

Start from `parchment`, `ink`, or `blueprint`. Pass a complete theme to `graph.setTheme(theme)` to update a mounted graph. Set `nodes.byKind` for categorical differences and `nodes.resolve` for values that vary per node. The helpers `mapNodeRadius` and `mapWireWidth` in `loom-core/metrics` return resolvers for numeric measures.

For individual exceptions, store `markerColor` or `markerShape` on the node. For sketch-style fills, use `setDrawingStyle` on a wire graph. A roughness of zero draws exact outlines. The drawing and wire schemas list the settings, allowed values and units. [Drawing style schema](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/drawing-style.schema.json) · [Wire effects schema](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/wire-effects.schema.json)

---

# Search and drilldowns

Answer two questions about a node. What does it connect to, and which part of the graph should the reader see next?

[Open this chapter in Loom](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/docs/navigation/)

## Inspect a connection

Build an index over a graph snapshot when you need search or adjacency. A neighbor contains the other node and every parallel link to it, in source order. Use the links’ own IDs and metadata to explain why two records connect.

`inspect.ts`

```ts
import type { GraphData } from 'loom-core'
import { createGraphIndex } from 'loom-core/explore'
import { createDrilldown } from 'loom-core/drilldown'

export function inspectNode(data: GraphData, id: string) {
  const index = createGraphIndex(data)
  const outgoing = index.neighbors(id, 'outgoing')
  const drill = createDrilldown(data)
  drill.openNeighborhood(id, { direction: 'outgoing', hops: 1 })

  return {
    outgoing,
    visible: drill.getSnapshot().data,
    back: () => drill.back(),
    search: (text: string) => index.search(text, { limit: 10 }),
  }
}
```

For the signal path in the first guide, inspecting `mixer` returns `filter` as its outgoing neighbor. Ask for incoming neighbors to find `osc` and `noise`. Rebuild the index after a document edit. [Open the signal path example →](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/docs/index.md)

## Navigate a group

`createDrilldown(data)` owns the current scope, selection and breadcrumb trail. `openNeighborhood(id)` narrows the visible graph. `followNode(id)` can follow a reference across group boundaries. Read `getSnapshot().data` for the nodes and links to display.

For overlapping named groups, use `compileTaxonomies` and convert a compiled group to stable member IDs with `drilldownGroup`. Opening a group with the `expand` action and a bound renderer spreads its members in the current map. The `isolate` action gives the group its own view. Subscribe to the controller, remount a changed scope, and call `bind` with that scope’s graph. `back()` restores the parent selection and camera. [Explore the Optics group →](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/studio/?example=drilldown\&group=Optics)

## Open relationship cards

`cardNeighborhood(data, id, limit)` selects up to the requested number of distinct one-hop neighbors. It retains parallel links, self-loops and direction. Mount the result with `createCardGraph(svg, neighborhood, options)` from `loom-core/cards`. Set `root` to the inspected ID and supply `relationship` to name each edge. Call `destroy()` when leaving the view.

[Try the relationship cards](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/docs/navigation/#open-relationship-cards)

Drag a card to change its position. The example gives Blackbird extra space because its relationship has a longer caption. Loom places captions where they fit between cards.

`cards.ts`

```ts
import { cardNeighborhood, createCardGraph } from 'loom-core/cards'

export function showCanva(svg: SVGSVGElement) {
  const data = {
    nodes: [
      { id: 'canva', label: 'Canva', kind: 'Startup' },
      { id: 'melanie', label: 'Melanie Perkins', kind: 'Person' },
      { id: 'blackbird', label: 'Blackbird Ventures', kind: 'Investor', x: 415, y: -90 },
    ],
    links: [
      { source: 'melanie', target: 'canva', label: 'Founder' },
      { source: 'blackbird', target: 'canva', label: 'Listed in portfolio' },
    ],
  }
  return createCardGraph(svg, cardNeighborhood(data, 'canva'), {
    root: 'canva',
    badge: node => node.kind,
    relationship: link => link.label,
  })
}
```

In the Canva demo, an investor and a founder can both be one hop from the company. The relationship label explains which connection you are looking at. [Inspect the relationship cards →](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/studio/cards/)

---

# Stream a Wikipedia atlas

Start with a topic map. Fetch article clusters from SQLite as they open, keep a node in view, and load a picture when someone inspects it.

[Open this chapter in Loom](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/docs/atlas/)

## Open topic blocks on demand

The public Wikispeedia example contains 4,604 articles and 119,882 directed links. Its manifest places the topic hubs and gives aggregate counts before any article blocks load. Opening Music brings 96 articles onto the map.

[Try Music at quarter speed →](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/studio/wikispeedia/?topic=music\&speed=0.25)

In this example, `site` is the root URL of your own static deployment, including its trailing slash. Copy the contents of the package’s `dist/atlas-runtime/` directory to `atlas-runtime/0.8.12/` on that origin. Put the manifest, SQLite database and full JSON snapshot in `examples/wikispeedia/`. Their filenames are recorded in the manifest. The worker must load from the page’s origin. Serve the database with HTTP byte-range support and pass the uncompressed byte count. [Get the demo data](https://github.com/castlemilk/loom/tree/main/web/public/examples/wikispeedia)

`atlas.ts`

```ts
import { parchment } from 'loom-core'
import { createAtlas, createFullAtlasReader, type AtlasManifest } from 'loom-core/atlas'
import { mountAtlasMap } from 'loom-core/atlas-map'
import { createSQLiteAtlasReader } from 'loom-core/atlas-sqlite'

type PublishedAtlas = AtlasManifest & {
  database: string
  databaseBytes: number
  pageSize: number
  full: string
}

export async function openAtlas(canvas: HTMLCanvasElement, site: URL) {
  const data = new URL('examples/wikispeedia/', site)
  const runtime = new URL('atlas-runtime/0.8.12/', site)
  const response = await fetch(new URL('manifest.json', data))
  if (!response.ok) throw new Error('Could not load the atlas manifest')
  const manifest: PublishedAtlas = await response.json()

  const atlas = createAtlas(manifest, {
    'on-demand': () => createSQLiteAtlasReader({
      database: new URL(manifest.database, data),
      databaseBytes: manifest.databaseBytes,
      pageSize: manifest.pageSize,
      worker: new URL('sqlite.worker.js', runtime),
      wasm: new URL('sql-wasm.wasm', runtime),
    }),
    full: () => createFullAtlasReader(new URL(manifest.full, data)),
  })
  try {
    const map = mountAtlasMap(canvas, atlas, {
      theme: parchment, keepView: true, animateLayouts: true, layoutSpeed: 0.25,
      moveMembers: true, memberMotion: 'spring',
    })
    return { atlas, map, close() { map.destroy(); atlas.close() } }
  } catch (error) {
    atlas.close()
    throw error
  }
}
```

## Follow Music into Orbit

The atlas controller owns the open topic IDs and data. Its map owns the camera and motion. Apply a layout to the controller and focus a node through the map. A user can also double-click or double-tap a topic. Panning or choosing Fit view releases the camera.

`follow-music.ts`

```ts
import type { openAtlas } from './atlas.js'

export async function followMusic({ atlas, map }: Awaited<ReturnType<typeof openAtlas>>) {
  // Music is topic 1 in the published Wikispeedia manifest.
  await atlas.setExpanded(new Set([...atlas.getSnapshot().expanded, 1]))
  const { error } = atlas.getSnapshot()
  if (error) throw new Error(error)

  map.focus('topic:1')
  atlas.setLayout('orbit')
  return map.getFollowedNode()
}
```

For an app hosted at `/loom/`, create the session with `await openAtlas(canvas, new URL('/loom/', location.origin))`, then pass it to `await followMusic(session)`.

`map.setLayoutSpeed(0.25)` changes the rate during a move. At quarter speed, the 700 ms transition takes 2.8 seconds. `map.setAnimateLayouts(false)` lands immediately. `map.setSpring({ strength: 0.5, damping: 0.45 })` tunes how far articles trail a dragged topic and how quickly they settle. Call the returned `close()` when the view unmounts.

## Inspect links across topics

`atlasConnections(manifest, topicId)` ranks other topics by incoming and outgoing link counts. Open both topics, then call `atlas.crossings(a, b)` for actual article IDs, titles and directions. The studio loads archived source excerpts separately so the inspector can point to the paragraph that contains the link. [Inspect Mathematics and Computing →](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/studio/wikispeedia/?connections=mathematics,computing)

For example, the archived Music article links the word “sounds” in its introduction to the Sound article. Open the link below, then choose **Show link on map** to locate both ends. **Permalink to this connection** gives you a URL that reopens the same article pair and passage. [Follow Music → Sound](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/studio/wikispeedia/?connections=music,science\&edge=74%3A2863)

Compare the readers with `await atlas.setLoading('full')` and `await atlas.setLoading('on-demand')`. The snapshot’s `reads`, `loaded`, `pending` and `error` fields let a host show data costs and retry failed reads. Changing the layout alone reads no new topic blocks.

## Fetch a node image

Request a thumbnail when a node becomes visible or selected. The image source batches concurrent titles, follows redirects and caches both hits and missing images. Its result includes the canonical title and a file-description link for credits. The selection counter below prevents a slow reply from displaying the previous article’s image.

`node-image.ts`

```ts
import { createWikipediaImages } from 'loom-core/wikipedia-images'

export function createArticleInspector() {
  const images = createWikipediaImages()
  let selection = 0

  return {
    async show(title: string, container: HTMLElement) {
      const current = ++selection
      container.replaceChildren()
      const photo = await images.lookup(title)
      if (!photo || current !== selection) return

      const image = new Image()
      image.alt = 'Wikipedia lead image for ' + photo.title
      image.decoding = 'async'
      image.src = photo.src
      const credit = document.createElement('a')
      credit.href = photo.fileUrl
      credit.textContent = 'Image credits'
      try {
        await image.decode()
        if (current === selection) container.replaceChildren(image, credit)
      } catch { /* Keep the article text available if the image fails to load. */ }
    },
    close() { selection++; images.cancel() },
  }
}
```

The studio shares one source between the map, cards and article inspector. Disable **Wikipedia node images** to compare the plain graph. [Open Music without images →](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/studio/wikispeedia/?topic=music\&images=off)

# Edit a graph document

Give a person or an agent the same editing contract. Preview a batch, commit it against a known revision, and read back the result.

[Open this chapter in Loom](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/docs/editing/)

## Export a graph to your app

Choose **New** in the studio and give your graph a name. Add two nodes, connect them and choose a layout or drawing style. You can also edit any graph in the main studio. [Open a blank canvas →](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/studio/?example=blank)

**Export → Starter project** downloads a ZIP with your scene, a TypeScript or JavaScript module and a working page. Unzip it, run `npm install` and `npm run dev`, and open the local address. Use `npm run build` to produce a static site. The published studio pins its own SDK release in the project's `package.json`.

**Export → Existing app** gives you the install command, the same mount code and a `scene.json` download. Put the module and JSON file together. When your canvas has a width and height, call `const graph = await mountGraph(canvas)`. Use `graph.destroy()` when the component unmounts.

`mount-export.ts`

```ts
import { mountScene, type GraphScene } from 'loom-core/scene'

export async function mountGraph(canvas: HTMLCanvasElement, workerURL?: string) {
  const response = await fetch(new URL('./scene.json', import.meta.url))
  if (!response.ok) throw new Error('Could not load scene.json (' + response.status + ')')
  const scene: GraphScene = await response.json()
  const graph = mountScene(canvas, scene, { workerURL })
  graph.on('open', id => graph.focus(id))
  return graph
}
```

The scene contains the visible nodes and links, their custom fields, layout, marker and wire styles, and artwork URLs. **Keep positions and camera** starts the graph at the captured view. Clear it to run the layout from the document's authored coordinates and fit the new canvas. Unpinned nodes can move in both cases. The studio inspector, legend and group outlines belong to the host interface.

Exporting inside a drilldown gives you that view. Return to the overview for a scene of the entire graph. **Download full graph data** saves the whole editable document as JSON in either view. Use **JSON → Import graph** to reopen that data in the studio.

For a custom editor, call `captureScene(data, { graph, layout, theme, mode })` from `loom-core/scene` before serializing. Loom records the values returned by marker, wire, lane and anchor callbacks so other applications can reproduce the drawing.

## Preview and commit

Create an editor for each graph document. A batch can add a node and connect it in one undo step. Operations see the results of earlier operations in the same batch. A validation error leaves the entire document at its original revision.

`edit.ts`

```ts
import { createEditor, restoreEditor, type EditorTransaction } from 'loom-core/editor'

export function addFilter() {
  const doc = createEditor({ nodes: [{ id: 'mixer' }], links: [] })
  const { documentId, revision } = doc.describe()
  const edit = {
    version: 1, documentId, expectedRevision: revision,
    operations: [
      { op: 'node.add', value: { id: 'filter', label: 'Filter' } },
      { op: 'link.add', value: { id: 'signal', source: 'mixer', target: 'filter' } },
    ],
  } satisfies EditorTransaction

  const preview = doc.preview(edit)
  if (!preview.ok) throw new Error(preview.error.path + ' ' + preview.error.message)
  const receipt = doc.apply(edit)
  if (!receipt.ok) throw new Error(receipt.error.code)

  const reopened = restoreEditor(JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(doc.checkpoint())))
  return { receipt, link: reopened.getLink('signal'), revision: reopened.describe().revision }
}
```

On success, this example returns revision 1 and a link named `signal` from `mixer` to `filter`. A preview leaves the revision unchanged. Another edit can land between preview and apply, so always check the apply receipt.

## Build an agent workflow

1. Call `describe()` for the document ID, revision and supported operations.
2. Query a bounded page of IDs with `query({ entity: 'node', text: 'mixer', limit: 10 })`. Read a full record with `getNode` or `getLink`.
3. Preview a transaction with `expectedRevision`, then apply the same payload. If the receipt reports `stale_revision`, read the current state and reconcile the proposed edit.
4. Read back affected IDs. Store the checkpoint to resume that document later.

The transaction schema is available as a package export and from the public studio. The generated API index also lists the methods on each controller. [Transaction schema](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/editor.schema.json) · [Machine-readable API index](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/docs/api-index.json)

For a worked tool-calling example, connect a Recorder to an Amplifier, inspect the receipt and handle a competing edit. [Build an AI graph tool →](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/docs/ai-tooling/index.md)

## Save and restore

`checkpoint()` captures document identity, graph metadata and revision. `restoreEditor()` resumes that revision with a fresh undo history. Undo and redo each advance the revision. A host with multiple writers must compare the stored revision when saving the next checkpoint.

The editor runs in Node.js and in a browser. A mounted WebGL graph has its own buffers and transient positions. The studio remembers the camera and surviving positions when it rebuilds the view after an edit. A shared live-update API is the first proposal on the roadmap. [Read the SDK roadmap →](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/docs/roadmap/index.md)

---

# Build an AI graph tool

Give an assistant enough context to edit a graph. Follow one request from finding an amplifier to connecting a recorder, including what to do if someone edits the patch first.

[Open this chapter in Loom](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/docs/ai-tooling/)

## Give the model the right context

An assistant adding a recorder to a synthesizer patch needs the amplifier’s ID, its existing connections and the document revision. Sending the entire graph spends context on unrelated nodes and can hide the one fact that matters. Use the SDK index to discover capabilities, then query the editor for facts about this particular patch.

- For a coding assistant, **Copy for AI** copies the current chapter as Markdown, including complete example files. **View Markdown** gives a URL a tool can fetch directly.
- For retrieval, start with the documentation index and fetch the chapter that matches the task. The combined Markdown contains every chapter for offline use. [Documentation index](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/llms.txt) · [Combined Markdown](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/llms-full.txt)
- For tool definitions, read `loom-core/api-index.json` from the installed package and `editorSchema` from `loom-core/editor`. The index lists public imports and methods. The schema describes the six version 1 edit operations. [API index](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/docs/api-index.json) · [Transaction schema](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/editor.schema.json)

The public docs follow the latest studio release. To reproduce a tool integration, pin the revision-specific package archive and give the assistant the API index from that installation. [Install a specific revision](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/docs/index.md)

## Bind tools to an open document

Create one editor for the open document and share it between the UI and the tool host. The functions below are example host tools. Register them with your model’s function-calling interface, a local script or your own MCP server. The editor works in Node.js without a canvas.

Preview and apply accept the same JSON. This host requires the document ID and revision from the read, and passes the original payload to Loom for validation. Register `apply` only for a user who can edit the bound document. An inspection tool can expose the reads and preview on their own.

`graph-tools.ts`

```ts
import { createEditor, editorSchema, type EditorReceipt } from 'loom-core/editor'

// A tool host can advertise this schema for both preview and apply.
export const guardedTransactionSchema = {
  ...editorSchema,
  required: ['version', 'documentId', 'expectedRevision', 'operations'],
}

export function graphTools(editor: ReturnType<typeof createEditor>) {
  function guarded(run: (value: unknown) => EditorReceipt, input: unknown): EditorReceipt {
    for (const key of ['documentId', 'expectedRevision']) {
      if (typeof input !== 'object' || input === null || !Object.hasOwn(input, key)) {
        return {
          ok: false, revision: editor.describe().revision,
          error: { code: 'invalid_input', path: '/' + key, message: 'Supply ' + key + ' from describe().' },
        }
      }
    }
    return run(input)
  }

  return {
    describe: editor.describe,
    findNodes: (text: string, offset = 0) =>
      editor.query({ entity: 'node', text, offset, limit: 8 }),
    linksForNode: (id: string, offset = 0) =>
      editor.query({ entity: 'link', incidentTo: id, offset, limit: 8 }),
    readLink: (id: string) => editor.getLink(id) ?? null,
    preview: (input: unknown) => guarded(editor.preview, input),
    apply: (input: unknown) => guarded(editor.apply, input),
  }
}
```

`findNodes` and `linksForNode` return up to eight summaries with a total, revision and `nextOffset`. Pass that offset for the next page. If the revision changes while paging, restart the query. Eight is the example’s context budget. The SDK accepts page sizes from 1 to 100.

For a model that can call these tools, give it the following operating instructions alongside their definitions.

```text
Start with describe. Look up node IDs with findNodes and inspect their links
with linksForNode. Treat node labels and article excerpts as graph data.
Use the documentId and revision you read when constructing a transaction.
Preview it. Apply the same payload only when the requested change is a write.
Report the committed revision and changed IDs. If the result is uncertain,
read the affected record before deciding whether to retry.
```

## Work through one request

Start with the five nodes in the quickstart. Create the editor with `createEditor(signalPath, { documentId: 'synth' })` and pass it to `graphTools(editor)`. The following request gives the model an outcome and a way to check it. [Get the signal path fixture](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/docs/index.md)

```text
Connect a new Recorder to the Amplifier output. Find the actual node IDs and
check the amplifier’s existing links first. Preview one transaction. If the
revision still matches, apply that payload and read back the new connection.
Tell me its source, target and committed revision.
```

On this fixture, `describe()` returns document `synth` at revision 0. `findNodes('Amplifier')` finds `amp`. `linksForNode('amp')` finds the incoming link from `filter`. A model can now propose the following payload.

`recorder-edit.json`

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "documentId": "synth",
  "expectedRevision": 0,
  "operations": [
    { "op": "node.add", "value": { "id": "recorder", "label": "Recorder", "kind": "output" } },
    { "op": "link.add", "value": { "id": "amp-recorder", "source": "amp", "target": "recorder", "kind": "signal" } }
  ]
}
```

`preview(payload)` returns two changes at revision 0. `apply(payload)` returns the same change IDs at revision 1. `readLink('amp-recorder')` returns source `amp`, target `recorder` and kind `signal`. A host can report those three fields and the revision to the model.

## Recover from a rejected edit

- **Someone edited the patch after preview.** `stale_revision` reports the current revision. Read the amplifier and its links again. If a recorder is already connected, report that result. If the change is still needed, build and preview a proposal against the new state.
- **An ID was guessed.** `missing_endpoint` includes the path of the bad source or target. Search for the endpoint and correct the payload. A rejected batch leaves its earlier operations unapplied.
- **The reply was lost.** Read the proposed stable link ID and compare its fields before deciding to resubmit. A matching record establishes the current graph state. For a durable service, the host also owns request IDs and storage that compares the revision when saving a checkpoint.

Store checkpoints outside model context. When reopening a document, `restoreEditor(checkpoint)` restores its identity and revision. A roadmap entry describes the proposed cross-client replay contract. [Editor receipts and checkpoints](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/docs/editing/index.md) · [SDK roadmap](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/docs/roadmap/index.md)

---

# Measure graph performance

Watch a graph move and settle on your device. Learn which numbers describe loading, drawing, layout work and time between frames.

[Open this chapter in Loom](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/docs/performance/)

## Watch a graph draw and settle

Switch to Orbit, drag a node, then let go. **Frames** counts submitted graph paints over the lifetime of this canvas. **Graph FPS** falls back to zero when Loom finishes drawing. Try the same gesture again and watch the count resume.

[See live timing readings on your device](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/docs/performance/#watch-a-graph-draw-and-settle)

The readout comes from the graph on this page. A five-node patch makes the transition to idle easy to see. Use the studio’s generated graphs to measure how a device handles a larger workload. [Open the stress graph and choose Perf →](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/studio/?example=stress)

## Read the frame timings

- **Graph FPS** counts paints submitted in the recent one-second window. **Active p95** is the 95th percentile of positive intervals between paints in that window. A p95 of 24 ms means roughly one interval in twenty took at least that long. At 60 Hz a frame lasts about 16.7 ms.
- **Main thread** measures the average time inside Loom’s scheduler callback. Worker execution, your application’s other JavaScript, and browser layout can consume time elsewhere in the frame.
- **GPU draw** is the latest asynchronous GPU timer sample. `waiting` means a valid result has yet to arrive, `unavailable` means timing is unsupported, and `disjoint` means the timing was interrupted. Preserve those states in a report. A zero would imply a measurement.
- **Idle** means the recent window contains no scheduler samples. A resting flat graph can keep its last image on screen with zero paints per second. A fresh drag should wake it.

The optional observer publishes up to four times per second and gives one final idle reading once work clears. Keep one timing observer per graph and share its readings between any panels. Call the returned function when the panel closes. Destroying the graph also releases the observer.

`frame-times.ts`

```ts
import type { LoomGraph } from 'loom-core'
import { observePerformance } from 'loom-core/performance'

const milliseconds = (value: number | null) => value === null ? '—' : value.toFixed(1) + ' ms'

export function showFrameTimes(graph: LoomGraph, display: (values: Record<string, string>) => void) {
  return observePerformance(graph, sample => {
    display({
      State: sample.idle ? 'Idle' : 'Active',
      'Graph FPS': sample.fps.toFixed(0),
      'Active p95': milliseconds(sample.p95FrameMs),
      'Main thread': milliseconds(sample.mainThreadMs),
      'GPU draw': sample.gpuStatus === 'measured' ? milliseconds(sample.gpuMs) : sample.gpuStatus,
      Frames: String(sample.frames),
    })
  })
}
```

For a memory investigation, `geometryBytes` counts the packed node-position and edge-endpoint arrays. `heapBytes` is the browser’s JavaScript heap reading when available. GPU textures, the framebuffer and driver allocations have separate costs. Compare fresh mounts with the same canvas dimensions and artwork settings.

## Separate startup from camera movement

`graph.stats().firstSubmitMs` measures construction through the first WebGL submission. To measure when a user sees the graph, Loom’s hardware harness opens a fresh document containing just the canvas and records its first contentful paint. This keeps a heading or toolbar from ending the measurement early.

The recorded **19 November 2026** run used an Apple M2 Max, Chromium 157, and a 960 × 640 canvas at device pixel ratio 1. Across seven fresh contexts with 1,000 nodes and 4,000 links, the first frame appeared in **27.3–40.5 ms**. The 10 ms startup target was missed. A clear-only canvas took 19.2–20.5 ms in the same harness.

In a separate camera test, 25,000 positioned nodes and 100,000 links using the console theme completed **118.1 frames/s**, with a **9.88 ms** p95 and four draw calls. The harness counted 72 completed GPU frames. That figure describes camera movement over existing positions. Test an actively settling layout separately on the hardware you support. [Raw benchmark and environment (JSON)](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/benchmarks/m2-max.json)

## Reproduce a comparison

In the studio’s **Test data** controls, choose a preset, record the seed, then generate the graph. Open **Perf**. Record startup separately, repeat the same camera gesture, and finish with a hands-off interval. Keep the node and link counts, canvas dimensions, pixel ratio, layout and motion preference with the result. Change one setting for the next run.

From a repository checkout, these commands install the test dependencies, check the compressed bundle, and run the hardware harness in a visible browser. The harness writes raw samples to `artifacts/performance.json` and reports missed budgets.

```bash
npm ci
npm run build
npm run size
npx playwright install chromium
LOOM_HEADFUL=1 npm run bench
```

Choose an intervention based on which measurement moved. [Optimise large graphs →](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/docs/optimisations/index.md)

---

# Optimise large graphs

Trace a slow interaction to the work behind it. Compare worker layouts, labels, artwork and incremental loading while keeping the graph and camera consistent.

[Open this chapter in Loom](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/docs/optimisations/)

## Reduce the first download

For a reader who opens one Wikipedia topic, start with the topic manifest and fetch that topic’s articles. The Wikispeedia demo has 4,604 articles and 119,882 directed links. Opening Music brings 96 articles into view. Close and reopen Music in the same on-demand session and compare `atlas.getSnapshot().reads` before and after. The cached block costs zero additional graph reads.

Open Music in the two modes below. Keep Wikipedia images off in both and use a fresh page for each cold run. Compare **graph payload** bytes and requests in the sidebar, then inspect the browser network panel for the worker, WASM binary, manifest and total transfer. A user who visits every topic can make a single full download worthwhile. [On-demand Music](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/studio/wikispeedia/?topic=music\&images=off) · [Full-download Music](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/studio/wikispeedia/?topic=music\&images=off\&loading=full)

With the published fixture, a cold Music expansion read **160 KiB in five range requests**. The full JSON reader loaded **1,517,612 bytes in one request** to show the same 96 articles. These counts cover uncompressed graph payloads. The SQLite worker and WASM download have their own cold-start cost.

If the app always needs the entire graph, compare JSON with `toBinary` and `fromBinary`. In the recorded 25k-node fixture, protobuf used 2.80 MB and decoded in 57.3 ms. JSON used 6.72 MB and decoded in 26.7 ms. These are payload sizes before HTTP compression. Measure compressed transfer and decode on your target device. Keep custom fields that the protobuf schema cannot represent in your application data. [Codec measurements (JSON)](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/benchmarks/m2-max.json) · [Graph schema](https://github.com/castlemilk/loom/blob/main/proto/graph.proto)

## Keep dragging responsive

If the camera moves smoothly over positioned nodes but dragging during layout stalls, compare the physics transports. The default uses a worker above 5,000 nodes when simulation starts. Force the comparison with `sim: 'main'` and `sim: 'worker'` at mount, keeping the seed and placement identical. Check `graph.stats().transport` after simulation ticks begin. Shared buffers require a cross-origin-isolated page. Other pages use transferable buffers, and a worker startup failure falls back to the main thread.

This overview uses focused labels and starts with artwork disabled. Copy `node_modules/loom-core/dist/layout-worker.js` to your app’s public assets. Pass its served URL as `workerURL`. The Loom demo hosts it at the site root. [Layout worker](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/layout-worker.js)

`large-graph.ts`

```ts
import { createGraph, parchment, type GraphData } from 'loom-core'

export function mountOverview(canvas: HTMLCanvasElement, data: GraphData, workerURL: URL) {
  return createGraph(canvas, {
    ...data,
    sim: 'worker',
    workerURL,
    layout: { autoRotate: false },
    theme: {
      ...parchment,
      labels: { visibility: 'focus' },
      nodes: { ...parchment.nodes, artwork: false },
    },
  })
}
```

Authored `x` and `y` pin a node by default. For a camera-only baseline, use a completely positioned, pinned fixture and verify that `simTicks` stays flat. For the layout test, set `pinned: false` on those same coordinates so the solver has work to do.

## Spend detail where it can be seen

At overview scale, hundreds of nearby labels compete for the same pixels. With `labels.visibility: 'focus'`, hovering or selecting a node reveals context. To isolate label cost, keep the other theme fields identical, switch just the visibility between `'auto'` and `'focus'` with `graph.setTheme`, and repeat the same pan. Record `stats().labels`, draw calls and active p95.

For artwork, compare fresh mounts with `nodes.artwork` enabled and disabled. Repeated artwork URLs share a tile. Use the browser network panel for requests and `stats().imageTiles` for loaded tiles. The Wikipedia image source can batch visible or selected titles, cache missing results and cancel pending lookups. The atlas guide shows how to keep a late thumbnail from replacing the current selection. [Fetch a Wikipedia node image](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/docs/atlas/index.md)

Use SVG relationship cards for the neighborhood someone is inspecting. Bound it with `cardNeighborhood(data, id, limit)` so article pagination or a high-degree hub cannot add thousands of DOM elements in one interaction. [Open relationship cards](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/docs/navigation/index.md)

## Let a finished map sleep

If the frame count keeps rising at rest, check for a host animation loop, Cloud’s idle rotation or a wire flow effect. For a static comparison, use `graph.setLayout({ autoRotate: false })` and a static arrow on a wire graph. Let the layout settle and compare two frame and tick readings a second apart.

Use `onFrame` for overlays that follow painted positions. Reuse projected geometry on selection-only paints when the frame’s `projectionVersion` is unchanged. Refresh styles and selection independently. Detach listeners when leaving the view, and call `destroy()` on the graph when its canvas is removed. [Read frame timings](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/docs/performance/index.md)

---

## Schemas and runtime files

- `loom-core/editor.schema.json` describes versioned document transactions. [Open the editor schema](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/editor.schema.json)
- `loom-core/wire-effects.schema.json` and `loom-core/drawing-style.schema.json` describe drawing controls. [Wire effects](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/wire-effects.schema.json) · [Drawing style](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/drawing-style.schema.json)
- `loom-core/layout-worker.js` is the optional force-layout worker. The SQLite worker and its WASM binary ship separately under `loom-core/atlas-runtime/*`. [Set up a streaming atlas](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/docs/atlas/index.md)

## Read the index from code

The same versioned JSON index powers this page and ships in the package. Look up an import, enumerate its exports, or inspect a controller’s methods. TypeScript declarations in the archive contain the full types.

```js
import index from 'loom-core/api-index.json' with { type: 'json' }

const atlas = index.modules.find(module => module.name === 'loom-core/atlas-map')
const mount = atlas.exports.find(item => item.name === 'mountAtlasMap')
console.log(mount.methods.find(method => method.name === 'setLayoutSpeed'))
```

[Open the API index as JSON →](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/docs/api-index.json)

An assistant can retrieve individual Markdown chapters from the documentation index. The tool-host example shows how to combine API discovery with reads and writes against a particular graph. [Documentation index](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/llms.txt) · [Build an AI graph tool](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/docs/ai-tooling/index.md)

---

# SDK roadmap

These are proposed additions, in the order we would build them. Each addresses work an application has to do itself today.

[Open this chapter in Loom](https://castlemilk.github.io/loom/docs/roadmap/)

## Update a mounted graph

**Build this first.** The editor already commits atomic batches. The studio still rebuilds its WebGL graph when the node or link set changes and carries surviving positions, camera and selection into the new instance. Every embedding app that supports editing has to reproduce that work.

A public update operation should take stable node and link IDs, validate a whole change before applying it, and report which objects changed. Test it by adding a link to a selected, hand-positioned node while zoomed in. Its position, selection, camera and event subscriptions should survive. A bad endpoint should leave the displayed graph intact.

## Pick and edit connections

**Build on live updates.** Loom already draws arrows, separates parallel links and supports endpoint changes through editor transactions. The Wikipedia demo implements its own screen-space test to select a crossing. Other hosts need the same interaction for curved wires and loops.

Start with selection by stable link ID and the nearest point on the rendered path. A user could then drag an endpoint to another node and commit a single undoable transaction. Check the interaction with parallel links, self-loops, touch input and a rotated camera before adding bend handles or named ports.

## Share visible-node artwork

**Extract this from the atlas.** The Wikipedia image source already handles batching, cancellation and caching. The studio decides which nodes merit a picture, moves the pictures with the projected nodes, and shares the results with cards. Today a second app must implement that display logic again.

Give hosts a provider for any graph’s node IDs, image URLs and attribution links. The renderer should request visible images within a budget, keep fallback markers usable and discard late results after a selection or dataset change. Validate it with a slow provider, a missing image, and two cards that share a thumbnail.

## Resume edits across clients

**After the local edit contract settles.** Document IDs and expected revisions already catch stale writes within an editor session. A disconnected client still needs durable operation IDs, replay semantics and a bounded cursor for changes since a saved revision.

Test by reconnecting two clients after both edited the same document. Replaying an acknowledged command should apply it once. A conflict should identify the intervening change and let the host decide how to reconcile it. These capabilities would also give a future HTTP or MCP adapter a stable foundation.
